Class CursorContinuity

java.lang.Object
com.trevorschoeny.menukit.input.CursorContinuity
@Internal public final class CursorContinuity extends Object
Phase 16h — utility for preserving OS cursor position across screen transitions. Universal capture: every screen's removed() stashes the cursor; the next screen's init() (any screen, vanilla or MK or MKC or third-party) restores from the stash via the AFTER_INIT hook. Single utility class, no base-class coupling, no per-consumer opt-in.

Why universal capture

Vanilla / platform / OS layer moves the OS cursor to window center on certain screen transitions (consistent ~window-center coords on every InventoryScreen open in dev). Capture-on-opt-in can't help across vanilla→MK or vanilla→MKC transitions because vanilla screens (the LEAVING side) weren't opt-in candidates. Universal capture sidesteps that — every screen.removed() stashes, every screen.init() restores.

Why a utility class instead of base-class methods

Cursor continuity is a transition-behavior, not a property of any Screen hierarchy. Putting the mechanism in a utility decouples it from base classes and from per-consumer registration; the mechanism rides on Fabric's universal AFTER_INIT (which fires for every screen including vanilla).

Lifecycle semantics

  • Capture: every screen's removed() stashes the current OS cursor pos via GLFW.glfwGetCursorPos. Wired in AFTER_INIT for every screen so the listener exists before its eventual removed() fires.
  • Restore: every screen's init() reads the stash via GLFW.glfwSetCursorPos and updates Minecraft's internal MouseHandler.xpos/ypos via the accessor mixin. glfwSetCursorPos alone wouldn't update the internal handler state; the mixin sync covers that gap. One-shot, cleared after restore so subsequent unrelated opens don't get a stale pose.
  • HUD invalidation (Phase 17 follow-up): a per-tick listener clears the stash whenever Gui.screen() == null. Reason: HUD → first-screen-open should center the cursor (vanilla default), not restore from a long-stale stash left over from the last screen the user closed. Chained screen → screen transitions don't tick through HUD (setScreen is synchronous: remove → set new screen → init), so the stash survives those. Only an actual close-to-HUD frame invalidates.

Library-not-platform alignment (§0019)

Universal capture/restore is library-not-platform-compatible because it counters a platform misbehavior (vanilla / OS centering cursor on screen transitions). If the platform did the right thing by default, the library wouldn't need to act; since vanilla doesn't, the library compensates uniformly. There's no ambient behavior beyond "cursor stays where it was" — which is the intuitively-correct user-facing default.

  • Method Details

    • restoreIfAny

      public static void restoreIfAny()
      Restores the stashed cursor position if one is pending, then clears the stash. Wired from MKClient.onInitializeClient via registerRestoreHook() as a universal AFTER_INIT listener so it fires for ANY screen open (vanilla, MK, MKC, third- party — same behavior). One-shot semantics: cleared after restore so unrelated subsequent opens don't get a stale cursor position.

    • registerRestoreHook

      public static void registerRestoreHook()
      Wires the universal AFTER_INIT listener that does two things:
      1. Registers a per-screen capture listener. Every screen's eventual removed() call will stash the cursor.
      2. Restores stashed cursor. If a stash is pending (from the previous screen's removed() firing), teleport the OS cursor and clear the stash.

      Also wires a per-tick HUD-invalidation listener (see class javadoc "HUD invalidation"): whenever Gui.screen() == null, clear any pending stash so the next HUD → screen-open lands with vanilla's centering behavior. Chained screen → screen transitions don't tick through HUD and therefore preserve the stash for restore.

      Call once from the library's client-init entry point. Idempotent at the cost of duplicate listeners — but typically called exactly once.
